title: Why Can GPT Learn In-Context? Language Models Secretly Perform Gradient Descent as Meta-Optimizers
abstract: Large pretrained language models have shown surprising in-context learning (ICL) ability. With a few demonstration input-label pairs, they can predict the label for an unseen input without parameter updates. Despite the great success in performance, its working mechanism still remains an open question. In this paper, we explain language models as meta-optimizers and understand in-context learning as implicit finetuning. Theoretically, we figure out that Transformer attention has a dual form of gradient descent. On top of it, we understand ICL as follows: GPT first produces meta-gradients according to the demonstration examples, and then these meta-gradients are applied to the original GPT to build an ICL model. We comprehensively compare the behaviors of in-context learning and explicit finetuning on real tasks to provide empirical evidence that supports our understanding. Experimental results show that in-context learning behaves similarly to explicit finetuning from multiple perspectives. Inspired by the dual form between Transformer attention and gradient descent, we design a momentum-based attention by analogy with gradient descent with momentum. The improved performance over vanilla attention further supports our understanding from another perspective, and more importantly, shows the potential to utilize our understanding for future model design. The code is available at https://aka.ms/icl.
research_question: What is the working mechanism of in-context learning in GPT models? The paper investigates whether in-context learning can be understood as a form of implicit finetuning.
core_contribution: The paper explains in-context learning as implicit finetuning by showing a dual form between Transformer attention and gradient descent, and provides empirical evidence that ICL behaves similarly to explicit finetuning.
conclusion: In-context learning can be understood as a process of meta-optimization, specifically as implicit finetuning, and this understanding can inspire improved model designs like momentum-based attention.
key_findings: Transformer attention has a dual form of gradient descent.
In-context learning updates attention outputs and weights in a direction similar to explicit finetuning.
In-context learning covers most of the correct predictions made by a finetuned model.
In-context learning and finetuning pay similar attention to training tokens.
A momentum-based attention mechanism, inspired by the dual form, improves performance over vanilla attention in language modeling and ICL tasks.
limitation: The analysis is limited to Transformer-based architectures and does not cover other architectures like LSTMs.
The dual form is derived using a relaxed linear attention approximation, and the mechanism of standard Transformer attention may be more complex.
Due to computational cost, the analysis is limited to models up to 2.7B parameters and does not include larger models.
The analysis is based only on classification tasks and does not consider other task types like multiple choice or open-ended generation.
future_direction: Study in-context learning in non-Transformer architectures.
Investigate the mechanism of standard Transformer attention without the linear approximation.
Extend the analysis to larger models (e.g., GPT 13B).
Investigate in-context learning on other task types like multiple choice and open-ended generation.
